newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain denies judge's charge of massive corruption.
newsitem.headline: Spain denies judge's charge of massive corruption.

text.p: Spain's conservative government on Saturday denied charges by a senior judge of "gigantic" corruption in the country's political, judicial and economic system.
"I don't believe wholesale corruption exists in Spain," Justice Minister Margarita Mariscal de Gante told reporters.

The charges by Judge Javier Gomez de Liano of the National Court, a senior figure in the Spanish establishment, mirrored a warning by the country's top Communist that the boil of corruption is about to burst.

"In Spain, as in France or Italy, dozens and dozens of court investigations have brought to light a gigantic system of corruption that affects politics, the judiciary, finances and the economy," Gomez de Liano told a seminar in the northern region of Galicia on Friday.
"It has been, and in part it continues to be, a crisis of legality...which has tarnished a fair number of values and rules of the constitutional game," the judge added.

His comments come two weeks after a warning by Communist leader Julio Anguita that Spain was headed for a huge upheaval in a matter of months because a mountain of scandals from corruption to a "dirty war" on Basque rebels would end up engulfing politicians, police and the army.
Corruption has been a major theme in Spain for years as accusations of illegal party financing and personal graft piled up during the 13 years of Socialist rule which ended this year.

Mounting scandals, coupled with revelations about an illegal campaign against Basque separatist rebels which claimed 28 lives, forced then prime minister Felipe Gonzalez to call early elections in March which he lost.

His conservative successor, Jose Maria Aznar, used the corruption charges to maximum effect while in opposition to push Gonzalez out. Now he is in power, he says Spain should look to the future rather than delve into an unpleasant past.

Judge Gomez de Liano's own brother is the partner and defence lawyer of a disgraced financier, Mario Conde, who is accused by politicians of having bought thousands of stolen military intelligence files and of leaking them with deliberate regularity to incriminate former officials and enemies.

Gonzalez, now head of the opposition, has kept a low profile since handing over to Aznar but denies his critics' assertion that he is hamstrung by countless charges of corruption against close aides and by pending "dirty war" accusations against him.

His first interior minister and a senior general in the paramilitary Civil Guard are on trial in connection with the illegal campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murder. One third of those killed were cases of mistaken identity.
The courts are also probing charges that a fortune in secret interior ministry funds was diverted into private pockets and that the accused Civil Guard general trafficked in arms and drugs.
Gomez de Liano said corruption was so deep it had given rise to "a kind of parallel infra-state" managed by business and political lobbies, with its own codes of conduct.
